power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: Background: Low-calorie sweeteners (LCS) are consumed as sugar substitutes and may alter gut microbial composition.
Their effects on microbial functional pathways and cardiometabolic physiology in humans remain poorly understood, particularly among individuals with overweight.

We conducted a secondary analysis of an 8-week, single-arm pre/post intervention involving eight overweight young adult women who consumed sucralose-and acesulfame-potassium-sweetened Diet Pepsi three times daily.
Shotgun metagenomic sequencing of stool samples was used to profile microbial functional pathways with HUMAnN2.
Multivariable linear mixed models (MaAsLin2) assessed associations between pathways and metabolic biomarkers.
We hierarchically clustered nominally significant pathways into six representative groups and calculated Spearman correlations with interleukin-6 (IL-6), leptin, and HOMA-IR.
P values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure.
Biomarkers were measured using clinical chemistry and immunoassays.
Results: MaAsLin2 identified 33 microbial pathways nominally associated with the intervention (exploratory FDR ≤ 0.25); one pathway (PWY-5104) also met the conventional FDR ≤ 0.10 threshold.
Eighteen pathways were upregulated and 15 downregulated, with log fold changes ranging from -2.47 to 3.18.
The 33 pathways were grouped into six functional clusters.
L-alanine biosynthesis (PWY0-1061) was positively correlated with circulating IL-6 (ρ = 0.74; q < 0.01).
text.formatted: L-alanine biosynthesis (PWY0-1061) was positively correlated with circulating IL-6 (ρ = 0.74; q < 0.01).

text.text: Phosphopantothenate biosynthesis I (PANTO-PWY) was not significantly correlated with IL-6 (ρ = -0.46; q = 0.22).
Gut microbial functional analysis identified a positive association between L-alanine biosynthesis and circulating IL-6.
This finding complements previously reported taxonomic shifts in this cohort and suggests a potential relationship between LCS consumption, microbial function, and host inflammatory signaling.

Low-calorie sweeteners (LCS), including sucralose, acesulfame-potassium (Ace-K), aspartame, and saccharin, are consumed by about 41% of U.S. adults on a given day, primarily through intake of "diet" beverages (1).

text.text: LCS provide sweetness with no or few calories; yet their role in cardiometabolic health remains controversial.

Randomized controlled trials and prospective cohort studies often yield discordant findings, and a 2023 World Health Organization conditional recommendation advised against using LCS for weight management and prevention of noncommunicable diseases (2, 3).

text.text: >Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: This is a secondary analysis of data from a single-arm, pre-and post-intervention pilot study, previously described elsewhere (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?uWcxYf including participant baseline characteristics, recruitment, and original analyses.
text.formatted: This is a secondary analysis of data from a single-arm, pre-and post-intervention pilot study, previously described elsewhere (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?uWcxYf">15),</ref> including participant baseline characteristics, recruitment, and original analyses.

text.text: Briefly, eight overweight (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m²) young (ages 18-35 years) adult women were enrolled in the longitudinal study.
Participants were non-habitual LCS consumers and were instructed to consume 12 oz of caffeine-free Diet Pepsi, sweetened with sucralose and Ace-K, three times daily for eight weeks.
We collected stool and fasting blood samples at baseline (Visit 1, pre-intervention) and at week 8 (Visit 2, post-intervention).
The George Washington University Institutional Review Board (IRB #111635) approved the study, and it was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03125356).
All participants provided written informed consent.
We obtained microbiome sequencing data from the original study deposited in NCBI BioProject PRJNA995034.

Briefly, stool samples were collected from eight participants, processed for DNA extraction (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?H8h3zX and extracted DNA was then sequenced using shotgun metagenomics on an Illumina NextSeq 500 platform.
text.formatted: Briefly, stool samples were collected from eight participants, processed for DNA extraction (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?H8h3zX">15),</ref> and extracted DNA was then sequenced using shotgun metagenomics on an Illumina NextSeq 500 platform.

text.text: Functional pathway profiling was performed in the sequenced data using HUMAnN2 (v2.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?t3S6Vg) (8) with the UniRef90 protein database.
text.formatted: Functional pathway profiling was performed in the sequenced data using HUMAnN2 (v2.8) (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?t3S6Vg">8</ref>) with the UniRef90 protein database.

text.text: We extracted pathway relative abundance data for downstream analysis, both unstratified (community-level) and stratified by species.
This analysis used a linear mixed-model framework and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR; threshold ≤ 0.25).
We then used a two-stage pathway clustering and biomarker-correlation approach to systematically examine pathway and cardiometabolic biomarker associations.
Cardiometabolic biomarker analysis was performed using standard clinical chemistry and immunoassay methods by LabCorp (Burlington, NC) on an automated platform.
Biomarkers measured at both visits included high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), leptin, adiponectin, TNF-α, fasting glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, and triglycerides.
Biomarker data were normalized and clustered using HeliClust2.0 v2.0 (16).
text.formatted: Biomarker data were normalized and clustered using HeliClust2.0 v2.0 <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(16)</ref>.

text.text: PCA was performed to visualize variation in metabolic profiles across time points (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?eFdqNj.
text.formatted: PCA was performed to visualize variation in metabolic profiles across time points (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?eFdqNj">17)</ref>.

text.text: We tested associations among microbial pathways, cardiometabolic biomarkers, and host metadata (visit, age, race, BMI) with MaAsLin2 v1.26 (18) using a linear mixed model framework.
text.formatted: We tested associations among microbial pathways, cardiometabolic biomarkers, and host metadata (visit, age, race, BMI) with MaAsLin2 v1.26 <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(18)</ref> using a linear mixed model framework.

text.text: Before testing, we filtered pathways to those present in at least 10% of samples.

We fit each model on log 2 -transformed relative abundance, with standardized (z-scored) continuous fixed effects and a participant random intercept to account for the paired, repeated-measures design.
We applied no additional normalization, since HUMAnN2 output is already expressed as relative abundance.
Within each model, p values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method.
Two fixed-effect specifications were fitted.
• Model A took the form: pathway ~ Visit + Insulin + HOMA-IR + IL-6 + Leptin + Adiponectin + TNF-alpha + hs-CRP + Triglycerides + HDL + Sucrose + (1 | participant).
• Model B took the form: pathway ~ Visit + Age + Race + BMI + (1 | participant).
Model A served as the primary visit-to-pathway screen.
It supplied the pathways carried forward into the clustering and correlation analyses at a BH threshold of 0.25.
Model B supplied the demographic and BMI results reported in Section 3.1 and the Alistipes putredinis pathway-BMI results reported in Section 3.2, at a BH threshold of 0.10.
Model A included fasting glucose and insulin-adjusted dietary fiber, but the software dropped them due to collinearity.
We computed Spearman correlations between pathway cluster representatives and cardiometabolic biomarkers across all 16 samples.
Given the pilot nature of this study (n = 16), we also report associations with nominal p < 0.05 as hypothesis-generating.

text.text: At the full, unclustered scale (33 pathways × 12 biomarkers), a 1,000-permutation empirical FDR for the association between PWY0-1061 and IL-6 was q = 0.24.
After reduction to six cluster representatives and three pre-specified biomarkers, the same association passed per-biomarker BH correction (q < 0.01).

text.text: Eight young adult women (mean age 21.1 ± 1.7 years; mean body mass index 29.9 ± 2.8 kg/m²; 50% non-Hispanic White, 25% non-Hispanic Black, 12.5% Asian, 12.5% Other) completed the 8-week Diet Pepsi intervention (Table 1).

text.text: We analyzed the post-intervention cardiometabolic biomarker pattern of participants.
The PCA revealed that PC1 explained variance increased from 37.4% to 47.5%, while PC2 explained variance decreased from 26.9% to 21.7% (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The PCA revealed that PC1 explained variance increased from 37.4% to 47.5%, while PC2 explained variance decreased from 26.9% to 21.7% (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: This indicates a shift toward a more dominant post-intervention metabolic pattern.
Hierarchical clustering of the biomarker distance matrix showed changes in participant cluster membership between visits.
Cardiometabolic biomarker analysis identified hs-CRP as significantly higher in participants of Other racial and ethnic backgrounds relative to White participants (coef = 2.12, SE = 0.23, q < 0.001).
text.formatted: Cardiometabolic biomarker analysis identified hs-CRP as significantly higher in participants of Other racial and ethnic backgrounds relative to White participants (coef = 2.12, SE = 0.23, q < 0.001).

text.text: Leptin was significantly and positively associated with BMI (coef = 0.98, SE = 0.18, q = 0.0073), and hs-CRP showed a significant positive association with BMI (coef = 0.37, SE = 0.09, q = 0.0433).
MaAsLin2 analysis identified 33 microbial functional pathways nominally associated with timepoint (pre vs. post-intervention) at an exploratory FDR ≤ 0.25 threshold.
One pathway, PWY-5104, L-isoleucine biosynthesis IV, additionally met the conventional FDR ≤ 0.10 threshold (coef = 2.26, q = 0.095).
Of the 33 pathways, 18 were upregulated, and 15 were downregulated post-intervention, with log fold changes ranging from -2.47 to 3.18 (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Of the 33 pathways, 18 were upregulated, and 15 were downregulated post-intervention, with log fold changes ranging from -2.47 to 3.18 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>).

text.text: Pathway direction was strongly taxon-dependent.
All seven pathways attributed to Akkermansia muciniphila and all four arginine and ornithine biosynthesis pathways were downregulated.
Coenzyme A biosynthesis pathways attributed to Streptococcus parasanguinis were upregulated.

Pyrimidine deoxyribonucleotide pathways were mixed in direction depending on the contributing taxon: downregulated when Akkermansia-attributed, upregulated when Haemophilus parainfluenzae-attributed or community-level.
We also observed race and BMI associations for pathways attributed to specific taxa.
Functional pathways attributed to Alistipes putredinis were negatively associated with BMI.

These included phosphopantothenate biosynthesis (PANTO-PWY; coef = -1.06, q < 0.001), nucleotide biosynthesis pathways (UMP biosynthesis, guanosine and adenosine ribonucleotide synthesis; coef range -0.97 to -1.06), and peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathways.
text.formatted: These included phosphopantothenate biosynthesis (PANTO-PWY; coef = -1.06, q < 0.001), nucleotide biosynthesis pathways (UMP biosynthesis, guanosine and adenosine ribonucleotide synthesis; coef range -0.97 to -1.06), and peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathways.

text.text: The pattern suggests that higher adiposity is accompanied by a lower functional contribution from A. putredinis.

Multiple pathways were nominally enriched in specific racial and ethnic groups, particularly in the single Asian participant and the single participant classified as Other relative to White participants (n = 4).

Because these two groups comprised one individual each, the pattern is confounded with participant identity and is reported descriptively rather than as evidence of a race-or ethnicity-associated effect.

We retained pathways nominally associated with Visit at an exploratory FDR ≤ 0.25 threshold (BH-adjusted) for pathway and biomarker association analysis; we identify the subset that also meets the conventional FDR ≤ 0.10 threshold in Results.
Correlating 33 such pathways against 12 biomarkers would have meant 396 tests.

To manage this multiple-testing burden, pathways were grouped into six functional clusters by hierarchical clustering of their Spearman ρ correlation profiles across all 12 biomarkers (Ward.D2 linkage).
We selected the pathway with the highest maximum |ρ| within each cluster as the cluster representative.
This was reduced to 18 hypothesis tests (6 representatives × 3 pre-specified biomarkers: IL-6, Leptin, HOMA-IR) (Figure 3).
text.formatted: This was reduced to 18 hypothesis tests (6 representatives × 3 pre-specified biomarkers: IL-6, Leptin, HOMA-IR) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>).

text.text: We applied a per-biomarker Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction to the six p-values per biomarker.
The community-level superpathway of L-alanine biosynthesis (PWY0-1061 | unclassified) showed a significant positive correlation with circulating IL-6 (ρ = 0.74; q < 0.01).
text.formatted: The community-level superpathway of L-alanine biosynthesis (PWY0-1061 | unclassified) showed a significant positive correlation with circulating IL-6 (ρ = 0.74; q < 0.01).

text.text: It was the only pathway-biomarker association to survive per-biomarker FDR correction.

Phosphopantothenate biosynthesis I (PANTO-PWY | unclassified) was not significantly correlated with IL-6 (ρ = -0.46; q = 0.22) but showed a positive association with HOMA-IR (ρ = 0.55, p = 0.028; q = 0.17).
L-ornithine biosynthesis (GLUTORN-PWY | unclassified) showed an inverse association with leptin (ρ = -0.62, p = 0.011; q = 0.064).
These secondary associations were attenuated following FDR correction and are reported as hypothesis-generating.
This secondary analysis identified 33 gut microbial functional pathways nominally associated with 8 weeks of LCS-sweetened diet soda consumption at an exploratory FDR ≤ 0.25 threshold.
One of these, PWY-5104 (L-isoleucine biosynthesis IV), also met the conventional FDR ≤ 0.10 threshold.

Among the 33 identified functional pathways, the community-level superpathway of L-alanine biosynthesis (PWY0-1061) was significantly and positively correlated with circulating IL-6 (ρ = 0.74; q < 0.01).

This functional pathway-level analysis confirms the taxonomic observations of the parent study (15) toward a potential link between gut microbial functional activity and systemic inflammation markers.

text.text: Given the small sample size and single-arm design, caution is needed in interpreting the findings, which are preliminary and hypothesis-generating.
The association between PWY0-1061 and IL-6 has a biologically plausible, though unestablished, mechanistic basis.

L-alanine is the first amino acid incorporated into the bacterial peptidoglycan stem peptide, so higher microbial L-alanine biosynthetic capacity is consistent with greater peptidoglycan production and cell wall turnover (19).
text.formatted: L-alanine is the first amino acid incorporated into the bacterial peptidoglycan stem peptide, so higher microbial L-alanine biosynthetic capacity is consistent with greater peptidoglycan production and cell wall turnover <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(19)</ref>.

text.text: Fragments of peptidoglycan, known as muropeptides, can cross the intestinal epithelium and bind the pattern recognition receptors NOD1 and NOD2 on host immune cells.
This binding activates NF-κB and MAPK signaling, which drives macrophage production of IL-6 and TNF-α (9, 20).
text.formatted: This binding activates NF-κB and MAPK signaling, which drives macrophage production of IL-6 and TNF-α <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">20)</ref>.

text.text: Greater microbial capacity for L-alanine biosynthesis could therefore plausibly increase muropeptide shedding and NOD1/NOD2 engagement, offering one route by which the PWY0-1061 signal could relate to higher circulating IL-6.

The PWY0-1061 pathway has been found to be enriched in Enterobacteriaceae-dominated gut communities (21).
text.formatted: The PWY0-1061 pathway has been found to be enriched in Enterobacteriaceae-dominated gut communities <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(21)</ref>.

text.text: The PWY0-1061 signal in this dataset was detected at the community (unclassified) level, indicating that multiple taxa, including confirmed contributors Citrobacter freundii, Escherichia coli, Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Streptococcus australis, and Streptococcus parasanguinis, contributed collectively to this functional output, rather than a single dominant species.

This is consistent with a pathway-level rather than organism-specific association: microbial function is often more conserved across communities than the specific taxa that carry it out, since unrelated species can encode the same metabolic pathway, and a function distributed across several taxa can be more biologically meaningful than one traced to a single organism (22).

text.text: Whether this pattern reflects a response to the LCS intervention, pre-existing individual differences in microbiome function, or both cannot be determined from these data alone.

The association between PWY0-1061 and IL-6 observed here is consistent with the taxonomic pattern previously reported (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?PnS7T2 increased relative abundance of Gammaproteobacteria, specifically Enterobacteriaceae, alongside decreased Lactobacillales, following 8 weeks of sucralose-and Ace-K-containing diet soda consumption.

text.text: Enterobacteriaceae are known to constitutively carry the enzymatic genes underlying PWY0-1061, including alanine racemase and alanine aminotransferases.
Lactobacillales, in contrast, are associated with competitive suppression of Enterobacteriaceae through lactic acid production (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?6fsOoj).

text.text: This study observed both a nominal shift toward Enterobacteriaceae and elevated community-level L-alanine biosynthetic capacity.
That co-occurrence is consistent with prior literature reporting that LCS exposure, particularly sucralose, is associated with Proteobacteria enrichment in both animal and human studies (15, 23, 24).

text.text: The inverse, though non-significant, association between PANTO-PWY and IL-6 (ρ = -0.46) adds contextual interest.
Phosphopantothenate biosynthesis, i.e., vitamin B5 synthesis, is a precursor step in coenzyme A (CoA) biosynthesis.
CoA is required for SCFA production and lipid metabolism, processes associated with anti-inflammatory gut homeostasis (25).
text.formatted: CoA is required for SCFA production and lipid metabolism, processes associated with anti-inflammatory gut homeostasis <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(25)</ref>.

text.text: The functional capacity for phosphopantothenate biosynthesis was negatively associated with BMI in the A. putredinis-attributed pathways in this cohort (coef ≈ -1.06, q < 0.001).

text.text: Two additional secondary, non-significant associations support this inverse pattern.
PANTO-PWY also showed a nominal positive association with HOMA-IR (ρ = 0.55, p = 0.028; q = 0.17).
L-ornithine biosynthesis (GLUTORN-PWY), also detected at the community (unclassified) level, showed a nominal inverse association with leptin (ρ = -0.62, p = 0.011; q = 0.064).

Taken together, these nominal associations suggest that the same shift toward Enterobacteriaceae-dominated, pro-inflammatory community function, reflected in elevated PWY0-1061, may coincide with reduced Alistipes-associated, anti-inflammatory metabolic capacity.
None of these secondary associations survived FDR correction, so they should be interpreted cautiously as hypothesis-generating only.
The main limitation of this study was the relatively small sample size (N=8).
This limited the statistical power to detect modest associations.

Also, because shotgun DNA metagenomic sequencing directly assesses microbial gene content and functional potential, but it does not determine whether these genes are actively expressed or contribute to metabolic activity.
The observed functional associations therefore require validation through complementary approaches such as transcriptomics, proteomics, and/or metabolomics.
The study also has important strengths.
The pathway-clustering approach provided a principled strategy for reducing dimensionality and managing multiple-testing burden in a small-sample pilot setting.

In addition, prior evidence linking peptidoglycan-associated pathways to host immune and inflammatory signaling supports the biological plausibility of the primary finding: the association between PWY0-1061 and IL-6.
Functional analysis of the gut microbiome revealed that L-alanine biosynthesis is positively correlated with circulating IL-6.
This was observed in a cohort of young overweight adult women who consumed LCS-sweetened diet soda for 8 weeks.
This finding is consistent with the prior taxonomic shifts reported in this cohort and suggests a potential link between inflammatory signaling and LCS consumption.

Larger trials with longer LCS exposure durations (e.g., 6 months) will provide greater clarity on the effects of LCS on microbial functional features and their relationship with cardiometabolic biomarkers.
